/**
 * The shared element in the grid -> detail transition.
 *
 * Both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero render through this, so both carry
 * the same `view-transition-name`. When one unmounts as the other mounts, React
 * pairs them and hands the browser a single group that animates from the
 * thumbnail's box to the hero's box — the thumbnail appears to grow into the
 * hero instead of one fading out while the other fades in.
 *
 * `enter`/`exit` are pinned to "none" so this element only animates on its own
 * when it is genuinely shared. On a navigation where there is no counterpart —
 * the three thumbnails you didn't click, or a cold load of a detail page — "none"
 * drops the transition name, which leaves the image inside its page's snapshot so
 * it slides along with the rest of the page instead of breaking away from it.
 */
export function ProductImage({
  slug,
  color,
  className,
}: {
  slug: string
  color: string
  className: string
}) {
  return (
    <ViewTransition
      name={productImageTransitionName(slug)}
      share="product-image-morph"
      enter="none"
      exit="none"
    >
      <div className={className} style={{ backgroundColor: color }} />
    </ViewTransition>
  )
}

Done. All four behaviors are implemented and the build, types, and rendered output are verified.

## What I found first

Next 16.4 has **no `experimental.viewTransition` flag** — it was removed because the feature graduated. Next's bundled React exports `ViewTransition` and `addTransitionType` unprefixed, including in the `react-server` build, so these work directly in Server Components with no config change and no `'use client'`. `Link` also gained a first-class **`transitionTypes`** prop that forwards to `addTransitionType` inside the navigation's `startTransition` — that's what drives the directional slides.

## Implementation

**Shared element morph** — `app/ProductImage.tsx` renders both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero, so both carry the same `view-transition-name` from one helper in `lib/products.ts`. The key detail is `share="product-image-morph"` with `enter="none" exit="none"`: React resolves `paired ? share : enter` on mount and `paired ? share : exit` on unmount, so the clicked product morphs while the three you *didn't* click drop their transition name and slide away inside the page snapshot instead of breaking apart. I verified this branch in React's compiled runtime rather than assuming it.

**Directional slides** — `app/PageTransition.tsx` maps transition types to view-transition classes via the per-type record form, so direction is data, not duplicated CSS. Each route passes a distinct `name` (`page-grid` / `page-detail`); without that, both pages land in the same layout slot and React reconciles them as one element that merely resized, which animates as a resize rather than the exit/enter pair a slide needs.

**Suspense** — wrapping the *boundary* (not the two branches) makes fallback→content an update to a single group, so the skeleton cross-fades into content while the group's box eases between the two heights.

**Reduced motion** — layered so motion-free is the floor rather than an override: base rules use opacity only, `no-preference` layers the transforms on top, and `reduce` collapses the group geometry animation, which is the one piece of motion the browser applies with no CSS of ours involved. A reduced-motion visitor never has a transform declared for them at all. I also disabled the pre-existing looping skeleton `pulse` — it was unguarded, and a looping animation is exactly what that preference targets.

## Verification

`tsc --noEmit` and `next build` both clean. Server-rendered HTML confirms the actual wiring: `vt-name="page-detail"` on the detail `<main>`, four unique `vt-name="product-image-*"` on the grid with `vt-share="product-image-morph"`, and `vt-update="suspense-reveal"` on both boundaries. I also diffed the built CSS against the JSX and every class matches in both directions, with no orphans, and all six keyframes resolve.

## Three things to flag

- **I added `<main>` to the detail page**, which it previously lacked — it was rendering edge-to-edge with no `max-width` or padding. Without it the hero is a huge full-bleed square and the morph lands somewhere absurd. It's a real visual change beyond the strict ask, so revert it if that layout was deliberate.
- **Browser back/forward buttons get a fade, not a slide.** Those navigations bypass `<Link>`, and Next exposes no supported hook to add a transition type on popstate — `addTransitionType` has to be called inside the router's own `startTransition`. Rather than reach into internals, the `default` key gives untyped navigations a plain fade, which is why it exists.
- **The Suspense transition needs a client navigation to be visible.** React only animates a reveal that happens inside a transition, so on a hard reload the page streams without one. Grid→detail exercises it, since that route has a 100ms delay.

I couldn't drive a real browser — none is installed and no Playwright cache — so the animation timings themselves are unverified visually. Everything structural is confirmed. If you want, I can install Chromium and capture the transitions mid-flight to check how the durations actually feel.
